findings.source_passage: Oh, woe on woe! Oh, Death, why canst thou not sometimes be timely? Hadst thou taken this old blacksmith to thyself ere his full ruin came upon him
findings.why_it_matters: This apostrophe to Death is one of the most rhetorically distinctive and emotionally forceful passages in the chapter, with high voice-establishing and critical-engagement weight; its complete excision erases Melville's characteristic direct address and ironic lamentation.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the apostrophe to Death ('Oh, woe on woe! Oh, Death, why canst thou not sometimes be timely?') with at least the core contrast between the dead virtuous elder brother and the 'worse than useless old man standing.'

findings.source_passage: therefore, to the death-longing eyes of such men, who still have left in them some interior compunctions against suicide, does the all-contributed and all-receptive ocean alluringly spread forth his whole plain of unimaginable, taking terrors
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Death seems the only desirable sequel'
findings.why_it_matters: The full ocean-as-siren passage, including the mermaid voices and the multiple 'Come hither' imperatives, is the interpretive keystone of the chapter—explaining why broken men go to sea—and is critically central to the book's thematic architecture; the draft reduces it to a brief paraphrase losing nearly all its rhetorical and voice-defining character.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the mermaid chorus with its anaphoric 'Come hither' repetitions and the specific language about 'the guilt of intermediate death,' 'put up thy gravestone,' and 'till we marry thee'—these are not ornamental but structurally and thematically load-bearing.

findings.source_passage: as if toil were life itself, and the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart. And so it was.—Most miserable!
findings.why_it_matters: The source's syntactic doubling ('the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart') and the staccato isolated exclamation 'Most miserable!' are signature Melville prosody; the draft collapses this to 'toiled as if toil were life and his hammer its beating—most miserable,' losing the hammered repetition and the sentence's rhetorical shape.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the doubled phrase: 'the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart. And so it was.—Most miserable!'

findings.source_passage: Death plucked down some virtuous elder brother, on whose whistling daily toil solely hung the responsibilities of some other family, and left the worse than useless old man standing, till the hideous rot of life should make him easier to harvest.
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is the bitter ironic core of Perth's tragedy and a prime example of Melville's sardonic voice at its sharpest; 'the hideous rot of life should make him easier to harvest' is a textually distinctive phrase that critics return to.
findings.suggested_fix: Include at minimum the contrast between the taken virtuous man and the spared 'worse than useless old man standing, till the hideous rot of life should make him easier to harvest.'

findings.source_passage: his every woe unreverenced; his grey head a scorn to flaxen curls!
findings.why_it_matters: This closing image of the vagabond paragraph is one of the chapter's most striking rhetorical cadences and registers Melville's ironic indignation; the draft ends the paragraph at 'a vagabond in crape' and cuts the bitter final image entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Append 'his every woe unreverenced; his grey head a scorn to flaxen curls!' to the description of Perth staggering off.

summary: The draft commits two high-severity losses—the apostrophe to Death is entirely absent and the mermaid/ocean passage is severely flattened—plus multiple medium-severity voice flattenings; regeneration is required.
